I scheduled all 10 talks and saved the result to `schedule.json`. A separate checker run over the result found no constraint violations.

| Slot | A (120) | B (60) | C (30) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 09:00 | (room unavailable) | T10 choi (45) | T6 lee (28) |
| 10:00 | T8 park (90) | T4 kim (50) | T9 han (30) |
| 11:00 | T5 choi (110) | T2 lee (55) | — |
| 13:00 | T1 kim (100) | T7 jung (58) | T3 park (25) |

**Checks on the main constraints:**
- **Order:** T5 (11:00) comes before T1 (13:00), T4 (10:00) before T2 (11:00), and T6 (09:00) before T9 (10:00).
- **Shared audiences:** T1, T5 and T8 are each in a different slot (13:00, 11:00, 10:00). T2/T7, T3/T9 and T4/T10 are also in different slots.
- **Same speaker:** kim (10:00, 13:00), lee (09:00, 11:00), park (10:00, 13:00) and choi (09:00, 11:00) never have talks in back-to-back slots.
- **Availability:** jung is only at 13:00, and room A has nothing at 09:00.
- **Capacity:** every talk fits its room. The tightest fits are T7 at 58 of 60 seats and T9 at 30 of 30.

The constraints list only 10:00–11:00 and 11:00–13:00 as consecutive slots, so it's unclear whether 09:00–10:00 also counts. This schedule has no speaker in both 09:00 and 10:00, so it holds either way.

I wrote the solver as a script (`scratchpad/solve.py`) that tries every possible placement. It found only 2 valid schedules in total, and the one above is the first.
